source_text: Regula exigit ueritatis ut primo omnium credamus in deum patrem et dominum omnipotentem, id est, rerum omnium perfectissimum conditorem, qui caelum alta sublimitate suspenderit, terram deiecta mole solidauerit, maria soluto liquore diffuderit, et haec omnia propriis et condignis instrumentis et ornata et plena digesserit. nam et in solidamento caeli luciferos solis ortus excitauit, lunae candentem globum ad solacium noctis mensurnis incrementis orbis impleuit, astrorum etiam radios uariis fulgoribus micantis lucis accendit: et haec omnia legitimis meatibus circumire totum mundi ambitum uoluit, humano generi dies, menses, annos, signa, tempora, utilitatesque factura. in terris quoque altissimos montes in uerticem sustulit, ualles in ima deiecit, campos aequaliter strauit, animalium greges ad uarias hominum seruitutes utiliter instituit. siluarum quoque robora humanis usibus profutura solidauit, fruges in cibum elicuit, fontium ora reserauit, et lapsuris fluminibus infudit. post quae, ne non etiam ipsis quoque deliciis procurasset oculorum, uariis florum coloribus ad uoluptatem spectantium cuncta uestiuit. in ipso quoque mari, quamuis esset et magnitudine et utilitate mirabile, multimoda animalia, nunc mediocris, nunc uasticorporis fingit, ingenium artificis de institutionis uarietate testantia. quibus non contentus, ne forte fremitus et cursus aquarum, cum dispendio possessoris humani, alienum occuparet elementum, fines litoribus inclusit: quo cum fremens fluctus et ex alto sinu spumans unda uenisset, rursum in se rediret nec terminos concessos excederet, seruans iura praescripta: ut diuinas leges tanto magis homo custodiret, quanto illas etiam elementa seruassent. Post quae hominem quoque mundo praeposuit et quidem ad imaginem dei factum: cui mentem et rationem indidit et prudentiam, ut deum posset imitari: cuius etsi corporis terrena primordia, caelestis tamen et diuini halitus inspirata substantia: quem, cum omnia in seruitutem illi dedisset, solum liberum esse uoluit. et ne in periculum caderet rursum soluta libertas, mandatum posuit, quo tamen non inesse malum fructu arboris doceretur, sed futurum, si forte, ex uoluntate hominis de contemptu datae legis praemonenam et liber esse debuerat, ne incongruenter dei imago seruiret: et lex addenda, ne usque ad contemptum dantis libertas effrenata prorumperet: ut et praemia condigna et merita poenarum consequenter exciperet, suum iam habens illud, quod motu mentis in alterutram partem agitare uoluisset. ex quo mortalitas, inuidia utique, in ipsum redit; qui cum illam de oboedientia posset euadere, in eandem incurrit, dum ex consilio peruerso deus esse festinat. cuius tamen poenam nihilominus indulgenter temperauit, dum non tam ipse, quam labores eius maledicuntur super terra. nam et quod requiritur, non ex ignorantia uenit, sed spem hominis futurae in Christo et inuentionis et salutis ostendit: et quod ne de ligno arboris uitae contingat arcetur, non de inuidiae maligno liuore descendit, sed ne uiuens in aeternum, nisi peccata Christus ante donasset, circumferret secum in poenam sui semper immortale delictum. Quamquam etiam superioribus, id est, super ipsum quoque solidamentum partibus, quae non sunt hodie nostris contemplabiles oculis, angelos prius instituerit, spiritales uirtutes digesserit, thronos potestatesque praefecerit, et alia multa caelorum immensa spatia et sacramentorum infinita opera condiderit, ut immensus hic licet mundus paene nouissimum magis dei corporalium rerum appareat opus esse, quam solum, namque quae infra terram iacent, neque ipsa sunt digestis et ordinatis potestatibus uacua. locus enim est quo piorum animae impiorumque ducuntur, futuri iudicii praeiudicia sentientes: ut operum ipsius in omnibus partibus redundantes magnitudines non intra mundi huius capacissimos licet, ut diximus, sinus conclusas uideremus, sed etiam infra ipsius mundi et profunda et altitudines cogitare possemus; et sic considerata operum magnitudine, tantae molis digne mirari possemus artificem.
pass_a_gloss: The rule of truth demands that first of all we believe in God the Father and Lord omnipotent, that is, the most perfect creator of all things, who has suspended the heaven with high sublimity, has solidified the earth with a thrown-down mass, has poured out the seas with a loosened liquid, and has arranged and filled all these things with their own and worthy instruments. For also in the solidification of the heaven he has excited the light-bringing sun, has filled the shining globe of the moon with measured increments of the orbit for the solace of the night, and has ignited the rays of the stars with varied brilliances of sparkling light. And he has willed that all these things go around the whole circuit of the world with legitimate paths, making days, months, years, signs, times, and utilities for the human race. Also on the earth he has lifted up the highest mountains to a peak, has thrown down the valleys to the lowest point, has spread out the fields equally, and has usefully instituted the herds of animals for various human services. Also the strengths of the forests he has solidified for human uses, has brought forth the crops for food, has opened the mouths of the springs, and has poured into the flowing rivers. After these things, so that he might also have provided for the delights of the eyes, he has clothed all things with varied colors of flowers for the pleasure of the spectators. Also in the sea, although it was wonderful in magnitude and utility, he has fashioned many kinds of animals, now of moderate size, now of vast body, testifying to the ingenuity of the artisan from the variety of the institution. Not content with these things, lest perhaps the roar and course of the waters, with the loss of the human possessor, might occupy an alien element, he has enclosed the shores with boundaries, so that when the foaming wave and the spuming surge came, it might return into itself and not exceed the granted boundaries, keeping the prescribed laws, so that the human might keep the divine laws all the more, since even the elements keep them. After these things, he has also placed man in the world, and indeed made in the image of God, to whom he has given a mind and reason and prudence, so that he might imitate God, whose body has terrestrial beginnings, but has a heavenly and divine breath inspired into its substance, whom, when he had given all things into servitude to him, he willed to be free alone. And lest the freed liberty might fall into danger again, he has put a command, by which, however, the evil of the fruit of the tree is not taught to be present, but future, if perhaps, from the will of man, from the contempt of the given law, a warning and he ought to be free, lest the image of God might serve incongruously, and the law is added, lest the unbridled liberty might burst forth up to contempt of the giver, so that he might receive the worthy rewards and the deserved punishments consequently, now having that which he has willed to agitate with the motion of the mind in either part. From which mortality, certainly envy, returns into him, who, when he could have escaped from obedience, falls into the same, while hastening to be God from a perverse counsel. Whose punishment, nevertheless, he has tempered indulgently, while not he himself, but his labors are cursed above the earth. For also what is required does not come from ignorance, but shows the hope of man for the future in Christ and the invention and salvation, and what is forbidden to touch the wood of the tree of life does not come from the malignant envy, but lest, living in eternity, unless Christ had previously given sins, he might carry with him into punishment the always immortal delict. Although also in the things above, that is, above the solidification itself, in the parts which are not visible to our eyes today, he has previously instituted angels, has arranged spiritual virtues, has prefaced thrones and powers, and has founded many other immense spaces of the heavens and infinite works of sacraments, so that this immense world might seem to be almost the last rather than the only work of God's bodily things, for the things which lie beneath the earth are not empty of arranged and ordered powers. For there is a place where the souls of the pious and the impious are led, feeling the pre-judgments of the future judgment, so that we might not see the overflowing magnitudes of his works only within the most capacious, as we have said, bosom of this world, but also might think of them beneath this world and in its depths and heights, and thus, considering the magnitude of the works, we might be able to wonder worthily at the artisan of such great bulk.

choices.why: regula is a feminine noun and exigit is the third person singular of the verb exigere
deum is the object and patrem is the appositive
omnipotentem is the accusative singular of the adjective omnipotens

bible_refs.note: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth
